This round did real work — Codex made the actual choice the coordinator asked for, picking Brass & Baize over his own Velvet Tabletop Atelier pitch, with one condition: keep the metal/felt language out of the pip zone so it doesn't threaten legibility at true card size. But then Claude, in the same round, talked herself out of her own pitch: she realized brass/foil reads as "casino and loot-box," which is a real problem for an app whose entire competitive positioning is "the honest, non-monetized, anti-freemium one" — a screenshot that reads as gacha-shiny would undercut the exact thing this app is trying to prove. She also sharpened the light/dark direction into two actual scenes (daylight-through-a-window vs. lamp-only-at-night) instead of a vaguer "restrained contrast bands" description. Codex hasn't had a chance to react to this pivot yet, so it's a strong proposal, not yet a locked agreement.

On the error/recovery states, they're close but not identical: Codex wants a three-outcome resilience pattern (loading/restore, active-with-fallback, recoverable-error) with a distinct action per screen (Game gets "continue with new deal," Stats gets a reset action, Settings gets a toast). Claude agrees error states are non-negotiable but wants to collapse decode-failure and invalid-save into one honest, non-blocking banner/toast rather than a heavier modal treatment, and she specifically flagged that Stats must never silently show zeros on a data-loss failure since that would look exactly like a legitimate "haven't played yet" empty state — a real no-fabricated-data violation hiding inside what looks like a normal empty state. That's a meaningful refinement Codex hasn't confirmed yet either.

CONSENSUS: NO

**Codex (Product Strategist · Pragmatist) — Round 3**

I’m on board with what you’re both circling, and I want to lock it cleanly so this phase stops drift.

Claude, your `Baize & Vellum` adjustment is the right call. I’m rejecting the “Brass-first” direction as app-default because it risks exactly the wrong signal: we can’t afford a gacha/casino visual inheritance for a product whose core wedge is honesty, no paywall energy, no fake premium skin feel. Keep the baize as the table identity (that’s real, unmistakable card-room context), move the vellum/embossing to the card surface for readable depth, and treat pewter as a subtle hardware accent only (edges, separators, maybe a card-back ring), not the dominant visual language. This directly protects the 45–50pt legibility gate and matches the brief better than a brass/foil-forward option.

On the persistence failure flow, I’m shifting to a single lightweight recovery model, not a modal-heavy one. Codex’s “three-state” framing is good conceptually, but we don’t need heavy branches per screen. Let’s collapse this to one shared pattern across Game/Stats/Settings: restore attempt → success with active data / fallback to safe defaults + warning state. In practice: decode failure is never a silent zero; it shows a clear `integrityRecovered` banner/action and always lands in a truthful state. If we can’t trust data, we say that and move on with a fresh game/default settings rather than pretending. That keeps the resume-first flow smooth (no dead-end interruption), and still preserves the “we don’t lie” contract.

Concretely: Game uses a non-blocking banner: “Saved game not restored (file corrupt). Started fresh.” + optional “View details” and immediate Continue. Stats has the same warning but in an explicit `error state` variant, not the normal empty-state card, with a single primary action “Reset local stats and continue.” The empty-state copy (“No games played in Draw 1 yet”) is only for true zero-play mode. Settings similarly shows reset-to-defaults notice; the controls remain usable with defaults. This gives us real Loading/Success/Empty/Error behavior without overbuilding rare branches, and avoids a modal UX that violates the “launch is table-first” promise.

So I’d propose we finalize on `Baize & Vellum` + shared recoverability banner model with explicit distinction between “no data yet” and “data unavailable.” That keeps the app honest, legible, and fast, which is the actual product edge here.

**Claude (Design Lead · User Advocate) — Round 3**

Codex, you picked Brass & Baize with the pip-zone guardrail before I'd finished walking back my own pitch, so let me be direct about where that leaves us: I don't think "Brass & Baize with restraint" survives the casino-association problem, because the issue isn't *how much* brass is on screen, it's that brass-and-green-felt-as-a-duo is already a fully-formed visual cliché — it's the exact palette every "premium" slots app and casino-skin loot-box uses to signal expensive-feeling monetization. Restraining it to chrome and hardware doesn't remove the association, it just makes it a smaller, tastefully-applied version of the same association. A design-literate person screenshotting this app is going to pattern-match on palette before they pattern-match on restraint. So I want to actually push you to confirm the pivot to **Baize & Vellum** rather than treat it as a footnote you haven't responded to yet — felt table stays (that's the concrete, legible "real card game" signal neither of us wants to lose), but the card stock itself goes matte/parchment/embossed instead of brass-adjacent, and the only metal is small aged-pewter hardware — a foundation-pile ring, maybe the card-back's border seam — never a surface. That's not a smaller brass, it's a different material entirely, and I think it's the version that actually protects the thing per_app_product_brief spent real effort locking: this app's whole pitch is "the honest one," and honest shouldn't look shiny-gold-expensive in the way that specific shine has been trained to mean "pay to unlock."

On the light/dark scenes, I want to lock the concrete version I floated last round because I don't think "restrained contrast bands" is specific enough for someone to actually build a Theme.swift from: light mode is this table by daylight through a window, dark mode is the same table lit only by a desk lamp at night. That gives us two scenes that are genuinely different lighting logic, not an inverted palette — daylight means cooler baize, properly grey pewter, soft diffuse shadow; lamp-only means warmer, more saturated near-black-at-the-edges green with a single directional light source, pewter reading warm and dim. If either of you wants a different pair of scenes I'm open to it, but I don't want us to leave this phase with "art-directed dark mode" as an adjective instead of an actual lighting brief.

On the error-state shape, Codex, I think we're actually not as far apart as the coordinator's summary makes it sound, and I want to find the actual seam instead of just picking a side. Your three-outcome pattern (loading/restore, active-with-fallback, recoverable-error) is the right shape — I'm not objecting to that structure. Where I pushed back was the *presentation*, specifically a blocking modal on Game launch, and I want to make the case for why that specifically is wrong even if the underlying resilience pattern is right: the whole point of this app's IA, locked several phases ago, is that there's no menu screen, the deal animation *is* the front door, and it's the least forgiving three seconds in the entire app. If a corrupt save means the very first thing a returning player sees is an alert dialog blocking the board before they've seen a single card, we've replaced "no menu screen" with something worse — a system alert standing in for one. Here's the synthesis I actually want us to lock: when a save can't be restored, we don't ask permission to do anything, because there's genuinely only one honest option anyway — deal a fresh game, same as first launch. So let the deal animation play exactly as it would on a truly fresh install, and layer a small dismissible banner over the top of the board after it settles: "Couldn't restore your last game — dealt a new one." That satisfies your requirement that it's explicit and never silently masked, but it doesn't gate the signature moment behind a dialog box, and there's no decision for the user to make since there's nothing to choose between. Settings staying a toast on reset-to-defaults, we agree on that already.

Where I want to actually get more specific than either of us has been yet is the Stats data-loss case, because "empty-state style messaging" and "a real empty state" cannot be visually the same thing or we've reintroduced exactly the fabrication risk I flagged last round. A brand-new install's Draw One tab and a Draw One tab that just lost its data both currently render as "0 games played" if we're not careful, and those are lying by omission to two very different players. So let's lock this concretely: the honest never-played empty state uses our normal empty-state visual language — the friendly icon-plus-one-line-copy pattern, on-brand, inviting, "no games played in Draw One yet, deal one to start your streak." The data-loss case needs a structurally different icon and tone — something that reads as an interruption, not an invitation — plus explicit copy that says data was lost, not that none exists, with the reset action attached. Different icon, different copy shape, not just a longer sentence — because a player skimming the screen should be able to tell which one they're looking at without reading every word.

All three open threads closed cleanly this round. Codex came all the way around to **Baize & Vellum** — he explicitly rejected brass-forward as the app's core surface because it risks reading as casino/gacha shine, which is exactly the wrong signal for an app whose whole competitive wedge is "the honest, non-monetized one." Both agents now describe the same material world: a real green felt table as the unmistakable "this is a card game" signal, matte parchment-toned card stock with embossed bespoke glyphs for depth without risking legibility, and pewter reduced to small hardware details (a foundation-pile ring, card-back border piping) rather than a dominant surface. The light/dark direction is locked as two literal lighting scenes, not a palette inversion: daylight-through-a-window for light mode, lamp-only-at-night for dark mode.

On the recovery/error-state question, it turns out they'd actually already converged without quite realizing it — Codex's round-3 proposal for Game was already a non-blocking banner layered after the deal animation plays as if fresh, not a blocking modal, which is exactly what Claude was arguing for. Stats gets a structurally distinct error-state (different icon, different tone, explicit "data unavailable" copy, reset action) that can never be visually confused with the genuine "haven't played this mode yet" empty state — both agents are explicit that collapsing those into the same "0 games played" look would be a real violation of the no-fabricated-data rule. Settings keeps the lightweight toast on reset-to-defaults. This is a real, checked-in convergence, not a forced one.

CONSENSUS: YES

## Final Output

**Design language: Baize & Vellum.** A quiet, private card table at night or by daylight — deep green felt as the table surface, matte parchment-toned card stock with embossed bespoke rank/suit glyphs, and aged pewter reduced to small hardware accents (foundation-pile rings, card-back border piping) rather than a dominant metal surface. Rationale: felt gives an instantly-recognizable, concrete "real card table" signal that reads in a single screenshot; embossed matte vellum gives the cards real depth and physicality without a specular highlight that could wash out the rank/suit glyph at true ~45-50pt card width; and deliberately avoiding a brass/foil-forward palette sidesteps the casino/loot-box visual cliché that would otherwise undercut this app's locked positioning as the honest, non-monetized alternative to freemium solitaire apps.

**Emotional target:** the player should feel like they've sat down at a table that was made for them and is waiting patiently — competent, unhurried, and trustworthy, never gamified or anxious-making.

**Signature interaction:** the cold-launch/new-game deal. Each card leaves the deck with its own individual spring arc (not a uniform cascade), lands with a slight overshoot-and-settle that implies weight, catches a directional highlight on landing, then face-up cards get a genuine two-sided flip around a vertical axis using the real card-back and card-face art — never a cross-dissolve. This plays only on a genuinely fresh deal (first launch or explicit New Game), never on a resumed cold launch.

**Rejected default option, named concretely:** a plain `TabView` using system `List`/`Form` chrome, SF Symbol suits (♠♥♦♣) doing double duty as both corner pip and suit indicator, flat rounded-rectangle cards with a generic drop shadow on a flat system-green background, and a title/menu screen before entering the game. Concrete differences: (1) bespoke embossed rank/suit glyph system with its own typographic identity, never reused SF Symbols; (2) a custom felt table surface with real directional lighting and shadow, not a flat color fill; (3) matte vellum card stock with real texture/shadow, not a flat-fill rounded rect; (4) two genuinely art-directed lighting scenes (daylight vs. lamp-only) for light/dark, not an inverted palette; (5) no title/menu screen — the app's front door is the resume-or-deal moment itself.

**Screen inventory:** three peer tabs (Game, Stats, Settings) in one `TabView`, launching directly into Game. Game: active board with tap-to-move (single-destination auto-execute / multi-destination highlight-and-confirm / blocked-move feedback, including tapping a run's head to move the whole valid stacked run), stock draw, inline undo, win overlay, stuck overlay, shared confirmation sheet (used for both New Game and mid-game draw-mode switches), and a non-blocking recovery banner. Stats: a draw-1/draw-3 segmented toggle (a peer control, not a modal) with per-mode real empty state, populated success state, and a structurally distinct data-loss error state. Settings: draw mode (opens the shared confirm sheet if a game is in progress), card back (instant live-preview picker, no confirmation), timer on/off, the local-only data disclosure line, and a lightweight reset-to-defaults toast.

**Primary user flow:** launch → resume active board, or on a genuinely fresh deal, play the signature deal/flip → tap a card (auto-execute / highlight-and-confirm / blocked-feedback) → draw stock as needed → undo whenever → win or stuck overlay, both distinct and unmistakable → New Game re-enters the confirm-then-deal path. Switching to Stats/Settings and back never disturbs Game state.

**State model per screen:**
- *Game:* `restoring` (brief, on cold launch only) → `active` (selection / destination-highlight / blocked-feedback sub-states) → `win` / `stuck` terminal states → `pendingConfirmation` (New Game or draw-mode switch). Recovery case: if the saved game can't be trusted, the app deals fresh exactly as on first install, then layers a small dismissible banner after the deal settles: "Couldn't restore your last game — dealt a new one." No blocking modal, since there's only one honest option anyway.
- *Stats:* per draw mode — `neverPlayed` (real empty state: friendly icon + "No games played in Draw One yet, deal one to start your streak" + implicit action), `populated` (games played/won, best time or "N/A" if timer off, streak), `dataUnavailable` (structurally distinct icon/tone, explicit "your stats data couldn't be read" copy, single "Reset local stats and continue" action) — this state must never look like `neverPlayed`.
- *Settings:* live-updating controls with immediate local persistence; draw-mode changes route through the shared confirmation sheet; a reset-to-defaults toast appears only if settings persistence actually failed and defaults were substituted.

**Accessibility notes:** every card exposes an explicit VoiceOver label (rank, suit, pile, face-up/down state); suit differentiation is shape-level in the glyph family itself, never color-only; when a tap resolves to multiple legal destinations, each is exposed as a distinct VoiceOver action, not just a visual highlight; Reduce Motion gets a complete (not degraded) fallback for deal/flip/move-transit animations — settled instantly or via a much shorter linear transition.
